title: Physics
target_note: 27 questions in 40 minutes, with g = 10 m/s² throughout. The physics is GCSE; the marks are lost to units. Most wrong options here are the right number in the wrong unit, or off by the factor the question invites.

questions.stem_html:
A charge of 4.8 C flows past a point.

How many electrons is that? (electron charge = 1.6 × 10−19 C)
questions.solution_html:
Number = total chargecharge per electron = 4.81.6 × 10−19.

4.8 ÷ 1.6 = 3, and dividing by 10−19 multiplies by 1019: 3.0 × 10¹⁹.

Dividing by a negative power of ten raises the index. Getting 10−19 in the answer means the division went the wrong way.

traps.D: The charge itself with an index attached.
traps.E: One power of ten too many.
traps.F: Multiplied instead of divided, and the index sign kept.

questions.detail: Charge to a count of electrons

questions.stem_html:
A 12 V supply drives a current of 2 A through a heater for 5 minutes.

How much energy is transferred?
questions.solution_html:
E = VIt, and t must be in seconds: 5 minutes = 300 s.

12 × 2 × 300 = 7200 J.

Leaving t as 5 gives 120 J, which is in the list. Every energy formula in this paper wants seconds.

traps.A: VI — the power in watts, not the energy.
traps.C: 12 × 120 — a partial conversion.
traps.D: Half the answer, or 12 × 300.
traps.F: Time taken as 600 s.

questions.detail: Energy delivered over a stated time

questions.stem_html:
A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor are connected in parallel, and that combination is in series with a 4 Ω resistor across a 12 V supply.

What current flows from the supply?
questions.solution_html:
Parallel pair: 1R = 16 + 13 = 12, so R = 2 Ω.

Total resistance 2 + 4 = 6 Ω, so I = 126 = 2 A.

Adding all three (13 Ω) gives 0.92 A. The parallel pair is always smaller than either resistor in it — a useful sanity check.

traps.A: Using 9 Ω — the 6 and 3 added rather than combined in parallel.
traps.C: Using the 4 Ω resistor alone.
traps.D: Using the 2 Ω parallel pair alone.
traps.F: Total resistance taken as 1.5 Ω.

questions.stem_html:
A filament lamp draws 2 A when connected across 12 V.

What is its resistance at that moment?
questions.solution_html:
R = VI = 122 = 6 Ω.

'At that moment' matters: a filament's resistance rises with temperature, so this value does not hold at other currents. The question asks only for the ratio at this one reading.

traps.F: VI — that is power in watts.

questions.stem_html:
A 12 V supply is connected across a 2 kΩ thermistor in series with a 4 kΩ resistor.

What is the voltage across the 4 kΩ resistor?
questions.solution_html:
The same current flows through both, so the voltages divide in the ratio of the resistances.

Across the 4 kΩ: 12 × 42 + 4 = 8 V.

The larger resistance takes the larger share. Getting 4 V means the fraction was the wrong way up.

traps.B: 12 × 2/6 — the voltage across the thermistor instead.
traps.C: Splitting the supply equally, as if the resistances matched.
traps.F: The whole supply — the thermistor takes some of it.

questions.stem_html:
A transformer has 1200 turns on the primary and 50 turns on the secondary. The primary is connected to 240 V a.c.

What is the secondary voltage?
questions.solution_html:
VsVp = NsNp, so Vs = 240 × 501200 = 10 V.

Fewer turns on the secondary means a step-down: the answer must be well below 240 V. Anything larger has the ratio inverted.

traps.C: Dividing by 10 — the ratio approximated too crudely.
traps.E: The ratio inverted and then halved.
traps.F: 240 × 1200/50 — the ratio fully inverted.

questions.stem_html:
Electricity is sent along a cable of fixed resistance. The current is halved and the cable is unchanged.

The power wasted in the cable becomes
questions.solution_html:
Power wasted in the cable is I2R.

Halving I multiplies I2 by 14, so the loss falls to one quarter.

Use I2R, not V2/R — it is the current through the cable that is known, not the voltage across it. That choice is the entire reason the grid transmits at high voltage.

traps.A: I³R — the power law is squared, not cubed.
traps.C: Treating the loss as proportional to I.
traps.D: The loss depends on the current.
traps.F: Doubling the current rather than halving it.

questions.stem_html:
A wire of length 20 cm carries 3 A at right angles to a magnetic field of 0.5 T.

What force acts on it?
questions.solution_html:
F = BIL with L in metres: 20 cm = 0.20 m.

0.5 × 3 × 0.20 = 0.3 N.

Leaving the length as 20 gives 30 N — a hundred times too big, and in the list.

traps.A: Length taken as 2 cm, or an extra factor of ten lost.
traps.C: BI only — the length omitted.
traps.D: The current, with the field and length dropped.
traps.F: Length in centimetres and an extra factor of ten.

questions.stem_html:
An a.c. generator turning at 50 Hz produces a peak emf of 5 V.

It is now turned at 100 Hz. What is the new peak emf?
questions.solution_html:
The induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux, which is proportional to the rotation rate.

Doubling the rate doubles the peak emf: 10 V.

The frequency of the output doubles too. Both double together — it is the same cause.

traps.B: Unchanged — but the flux now changes twice as fast.
traps.C: An average of the two, not a proportionality.
traps.E: Squaring the ratio; emf is proportional to the rate, not its square.
traps.F: 5² — a confusion with a power relationship.

questions.stem_html:
A car travels at a constant 20 m/s for 5 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest over the next 4 s.

How far does it travel in total?
questions.solution_html:
Distance is the area under a velocity-time graph.

Rectangle: 20 × 5 = 100 m. Triangle: 12 × 20 × 4 = 40 m.

Total 140 m.

The deceleration phase covers 40 m, not 80 — the triangle is half the rectangle it sits in. Forgetting the half gives 180 m.

traps.D: The triangle counted as a full rectangle: 20 × 4 = 80.
traps.E: 20 m/s assumed for the whole 9 s, roughly.
traps.F: 20 m/s assumed throughout and rounded up.

questions.stem_html:
A stone is dropped from rest and falls 45 m. Take g = 10 m/s2 and ignore air resistance.

How long does it take?
questions.solution_html:
s = 12gt2, so 45 = 5t2 and t2 = 9.

t = 3 s.

45 ÷ 10 = 4.5 is the tempting first move and gives the wrong answer. The half and the square both matter.

traps.B: Using s = gt rather than ½gt², roughly.
traps.D: 45 ÷ 10 — neither the half nor the square applied.
traps.F: t² read as t.

questions.detail: Time to fall a given height

questions.stem_html:
Two blocks, 2 kg and 3 kg, sit in contact on a frictionless surface. A horizontal force of 10 N is applied to the 2 kg block, pushing both.

What force does the 2 kg block exert on the 3 kg block?
questions.solution_html:
Treat the pair as one body: a = 102 + 3 = 2 m/s2.

Now isolate the 3 kg block. The only horizontal force on it is the contact force, so F = 3 × 2 = 6 N.

The contact force is not 10 N. The applied force accelerates both blocks; only part of it is transmitted to the second.

traps.B: The force needed for the 2 kg block alone.
traps.C: Splitting the 10 N equally between the blocks.
traps.E: 10 − 2, subtracting the acceleration from the force.
traps.F: The applied force — all of it would accelerate the 3 kg block alone.

questions.detail: Connected bodies and the force between them

questions.stem_html:
A 2 kg trolley moving at 6 m/s collides with a stationary 4 kg trolley and they move off together.

How much kinetic energy is lost in the collision?
questions.solution_html:
Momentum is conserved: 2 × 6 = 6v, so v = 2 m/s.

Before: 12 × 2 × 62 = 36 J. After: 12 × 6 × 22 = 12 J.

Lost: 24 J.

Momentum is conserved and kinetic energy is not — that is what 'move off together' signals. Answering 0 J confuses the two.

traps.A: Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not, in a sticking collision.
traps.B: Half the energy after the collision.
traps.C: A slip in ½mv² for the combined trolleys.
traps.D: The kinetic energy after, not the loss.

questions.detail: Energy lost in a sticking collision

questions.stem_html:
A 0.20 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds at 10 m/s. It is in contact with the wall for 0.020 s.

What average force does the wall exert on it?
questions.solution_html:
Momentum before is +2.0 kg m/s and after is −2.0 kg m/s, so the change in magnitude is 4.0 kg m/s — not 2.0.

F = change in momentumtime = 4.00.020 = 200 N.

The rebound doubles the momentum change. Treating the ball as simply stopping gives 100 N, which is in the list.

traps.A: The speed is unchanged, but the velocity is reversed, so momentum changes.
traps.B: Momentum change of 1.0 kg m/s — mass and speed muddled.
traps.C: Treating the ball as stopping rather than rebounding.
traps.F: Contact time left as 0.002 s.

questions.detail: Force from a change of momentum

questions.stem_html:
A 0.50 kg object falls through air where the drag force is 0.20v2 newtons at speed v m/s. Take g = 10 m/s2.

What is its terminal velocity?
questions.solution_html:
At terminal velocity the acceleration is zero, so drag balances weight.

0.20v2 = 0.50 × 10 = 5, so v2 = 25 and v = 5 m/s.

The drag goes as v2, so the final step is a square root. Forgetting it gives 25 m/s.

traps.A: Weight and drag coefficient divided the wrong way round.
traps.C: Half the answer, or weight taken as 2.5 N.
traps.D: Weight taken as 3.2 N.
traps.F: v², with the square root not taken.

questions.stem_html:
A spring of stiffness 200 N/m is stretched by 10 cm.

How much elastic potential energy is stored?
questions.solution_html:
E = 12kx2 with x in metres: 10 cm = 0.10 m.

12 × 200 × 0.102 = 12 × 200 × 0.01 = 1 J.

Both the half and the square are easy to drop, and the centimetres are easier still. Leaving x = 10 gives 10000 J.

traps.C: Extension taken as 0.2 m.
traps.D: kx rather than ½kx².
traps.F: x left as 10 cm, then halved twice.

questions.detail: Energy stored in a stretched spring

questions.stem_html:
A 2.0 kg ball is dropped from a height of 20 m and reaches the ground at 15 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s2.

How much energy has been lost to air resistance?
questions.solution_html:
Potential energy lost: mgh = 2.0 × 10 × 20 = 400 J.

Kinetic energy gained: 12mv2 = 12 × 2.0 × 225 = 225 J.

The difference went to air resistance: 175 J.

Without air resistance the ball would arrive at 20 m/s, not 15. The gap between those two speeds is the whole question.

traps.A: 400 − 375, from a slip in the kinetic energy.
traps.B: A quarter of the potential energy lost.
traps.C: Kinetic energy taken as ½mv with v = 15.
traps.D: Landing speed taken as 16 m/s, roughly.
traps.F: The kinetic energy on landing, not the loss.

questions.stem_html:
A motor rated at 500 W lifts a 20 kg load through 5.0 m in 4.0 s. Take g = 10 m/s2.

What is its efficiency?
questions.solution_html:
Useful work = mgh = 20 × 10 × 5.0 = 1000 J, done in 4.0 s, so the useful power is 250 W.

Efficiency = 250500 = 50%.

Compare powers or energies, not one of each. Dividing 1000 J by 500 W gives 2 — a time, not an efficiency.

traps.A: Using the work done and the rating without the time.
traps.C: Height or time misread by a factor.
traps.E: A guess; the numbers give exactly half.
traps.F: No motor lifting a load at this rate is lossless.

questions.stem_html: How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 2.0 kg of water by 10 °C? (specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg°C)
questions.solution_html:
E = mcΔT = 2.0 × 4200 × 10 = 84000 J.

Three numbers, one multiplication, and the only real risk is a factor of ten. 84 thousand, not 8.4 thousand.

traps.C: The temperature rise omitted.
traps.D: Mass and rise muddled.
traps.E: Mass omitted, or a factor of ten lost.

questions.stem_html: How much energy is needed to melt 0.50 kg of ice already at 0 °C? (specific latent heat of fusion = 340000 J/kg)
questions.solution_html:
E = mL = 0.50 × 340000 = 170000 J.

The ice is already at 0 °C, so there is no mcΔT term — melting happens at constant temperature. Adding a heating stage is the commonest overreach.

traps.D: The latent heat for one kilogram, not for half.
traps.F: A factor of ten too many.

questions.stem_html: What is the pressure due to the water alone at a depth of 2.0 m? (density of water = 1000 kg/m3, g = 10 m/s2)
questions.solution_html:
p = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 2.0 = 20000 Pa.

'Due to the water alone' excludes atmospheric pressure. Adding 100 kPa would be right for the total pressure and wrong for this question.

traps.A: One factor of ten lost, or g omitted.
traps.D: Depth taken as 5 m.
traps.E: Atmospheric pressure — the question asks for the water alone.
traps.F: A factor of ten too many.

questions.stem_html:
Equal volumes of two liquids, of densities 800 and 1200 kg/m3, are mixed.

What is the density of the mixture?
questions.solution_html:
Take 1 m3 of each. Total mass 800 + 1200 = 2000 kg in 2 m3.

Density = 20002 = 1000 kg/m³ — the plain average, because the volumes are equal.

If equal masses were mixed the answer would be 960, the harmonic mean — option B. Which quantity is equal decides which average applies.

traps.C: A guess between the two densities.
traps.D: The harmonic mean — correct for equal masses, not equal volumes.
traps.E: A weighted average with the wrong weights.

questions.stem_html:
A block exerts a force of 600 N on the ground over a contact area of 0.020 m2.

What pressure does it exert?
questions.solution_html:
p = FA = 6000.020 = 30000 Pa.

Dividing by a number smaller than one makes the answer larger. Anything under 600 has the division inverted somewhere.

traps.C: Area taken as 0.2 m².
traps.D: A factor of a thousand from the multiplication route.
traps.F: Area taken as 0.002 m².

questions.stem_html:
A shout is reflected from a cliff and the echo is heard 2.0 s later. Sound travels at 340 m/s.

How far away is the cliff?
questions.solution_html:
In 2.0 s the sound covers 340 × 2.0 = 680 m — but that is there and back.

The cliff is half that away: 340 m.

680 m is the total path and is the answer to a different question. The halving is the entire point of an echo problem.

traps.B: 1.5 s used, or three quarters of the path.
traps.C: The total path there and back, not the distance to the cliff.
traps.D: 3.0 s used.
traps.F: 6.0 s used.

questions.stem_html:
Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass of refractive index 1.5.

Which statement is correct?

options.B: The wavelength is unchanged and the frequency falls
options.C: The wavelength becomes 900 nm and the frequency is unchanged
options.D: Both the speed and the frequency fall by a factor of 1.5
options.E: The speed is unchanged and the wavelength falls
options.F: The wavelength becomes 400 nm and the frequency is unchanged

questions.solution_html:
The frequency is set by the source and does not change at a boundary.

The speed falls to 3 × 1081.5 = 2 × 108 m/s, so since v = fλ and f is fixed, the wavelength falls by the same factor: 6001.5 = 400 nm.

Frequency is the invariant at a boundary. Everything else — speed, wavelength — scales with the refractive index.

traps.A: That is the frequency divided by 1.5; frequency does not change at a boundary.
traps.C: The wavelength falls in the denser medium, not rises.
traps.D: The speed falls; the frequency does not.
traps.E: If the frequency is fixed and the wavelength falls, the speed must fall too.
traps.B: This has it exactly the wrong way round.

questions.detail: What changes when light enters glass

questions.stem_html:
A nucleus of uranium-238 (proton number 92) emits an alpha particle.

What is the daughter nucleus?
questions.solution_html:
An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so mass number 4 and proton number 2.

238 − 4 = 234 and 92 − 2 = 90.

Beta decay would raise the proton number by one and leave the mass number alone — option E. Alpha lowers both.

traps.C: Proton number reduced but mass number left alone.
traps.D: Mass number reduced but proton number left alone.
traps.F: Proton number raised by 2 instead of lowered.

questions.stem_html:
A sample contains 80 g of a radioactive isotope with a half-life of 6 days.

How much remains after 24 days?
questions.solution_html:
24 days is four half-lives.

80 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 g.

Four halvings, not three. Counting 24 ÷ 6 = 4 and then halving three times is the usual slip and gives 10 g.

traps.C: Five half-lives.
traps.D: 80 ÷ 24 — dividing the mass by the days.
